apex_basket.value_chain_position: Royalty and streaming pure-play - no operating costs, a direct claim on physical ounces produced by third-party mines.
apex_basket.physical_anchor: Holds royalty and stream contracts entitling it to a fixed percentage of the gold and silver ounces poured at partner mines.
apex_basket.thesis: OR Royalties owns contractual claims on the gold and silver poured at 23 to 24 mines it neither operates nor funds, turning 96.8 cents of every revenue dollar into cash with no exposure to the mining-cost inflation now eating into its producer peers.
apex_basket.cost_curve: Company-reported cash margin of 96.8% in the June 2026 quarter (the screen's 102.85% is arithmetically impossible - it carries non-cash mark-ups including a $54M gain on the Osisko Development stake - so the company figure is the one used), the best in a peer group that includes Wheaton and Franco-Nevada. A plus-or-minus 10% move in the gold price swings cash profit by plus-or-minus 9.7%: the downside 9.7% is exactly as large as the upside, because a royalty has almost no cost base to absorb it - but it takes that hit from the lowest cost position available in the sector.
apex_basket.contracting_reserve: Twenty-three to twenty-four paying assets with volumes already contracted out to 2030; the book grows by buying new royalties out of cash flow rather than by funding mine construction, so growth does not consume capital and no capex commitment sits between the company and its cash.
apex_basket.capital_discipline: Net cash - net debt of minus 0.25 times cash profit - with interest cover near 86 times. There is no mine-building obligation at all, which is the structural reason this model cannot repeat the sector's habit of building at the top of the cycle.
apex_basket.valuation_guard: Base fair value of $35.00 against a $31.19 price and a reconciled margin-of-safety reading of about plus 12% - the guard passes. Points come off only for asymmetry: the adverse case at $20.00 is 36% below the price, roughly three dollars of identified risk for each dollar of upside to fair value.
apex_basket.regime_fit: The precious-metals chain reads neutral in the cycle sidecar, so this seat is carried on its own merits rather than on a chain call. A royalty is the shape that survives a flat or falling metal best, because its costs do not rise when the metal does not.
apex_basket.phase_fit: The macro note describes a phase in which the bond market is imposing positive real rates, so payback speed beats resource optionality - that favours cash-generative royalty models in every metal family, and this is the purest one in the book. The same note calls monetary metals the family currently without a driver, which is a reason to hold the seat below a full unit rather than a reason to drop it.

wheel.rationale: Torque is the lowest in the book at 9.7% either way, so capping the upside at the $35.00 fair value costs little, and being assigned at $24.00 means owning a 96.8%-cash-margin royalty book a fifth below today's price.

apex_basket.decision_rationale: Cash margin of 96.8% reported on 8 July 2026 with 2030 volumes already contracted; nothing in the June-quarter disclosure touches the thesis, so the seat is kept at three-quarters of a unit.
apex_basket.skeptic_kill_fact: No kill fact survived. The two loudest bear claims verify against primary sources but one of them has since been answered by the company on the record, and the valuation anchors are stale by a week in the bull's favour. (1) Cost-curve truth holds: the 96.8% cash margin is the company's own filed figure - $94.7 million of cash margin on $97.8 million of revenue in the second quarter of 2026 (5 August 2026 release and 6 August call) - and a royalty company has no all-in sustaining cost to check it against, so the record's rejection of the 102.85% deterministic proxy is right. (2) Reserve/contract truth holds on the numbers but not on the rhetoric: Agnico Eagle's own releases confirm 60,000-80,000 ounces lost in the second half of 2026 and up to approximately 150,000 ounces a year in 2027 and 2028, and OR quantified its own share on the 6 August call at roughly 3,500 ounces in 2026 and up to roughly 7,500 a year in 2027-2028, about 18,500 over three years - the same arithmetic the bear did. But the bear's claim that the five-year outlook 'does not survive the arithmetic' is now rebutted by a checkable reason: the 2030 outlook is a 2030 endpoint, and Barnat was always scheduled to be mined out by 2028 or 2029, so the hole sits in the path rather than in the endpoint. Management reconciled rather than repeated a reassurance, which is precisely the development the record itself listed as the one that would bring an entry forward. (3) Cyclical-peak cheapness is the one bear point that survives intact and gets worse: gold is $4,436.50 today against the record's $4,154 anchor, and 96.8 cents of every revenue dollar drops to cash, so the passing valuation guard is a metal-price print. At today's $33.54 the enterprise is about $6.43 billion against roughly $362 million of cash earnings - about 17.8 times, the same multiple the record measured, because price and earnings rose together. (4) No hidden disqualifier found: no reserve downgrade (Odyssey set a quarterly production record and the operator's stated life of mine runs decades out), no permit or licence issue, and the opposite of dilution - roughly 1.6 million shares bought back and cancelled year to date, including about 1.0 million for $29.1 million in July after the Barnat selloff, which fires the record's own 'is the buyback finally countercyclical' test in the company's favour. The fifth acquisition (Murray Brook, $28 million, closed July) was funded from cash, not equity, so the bear's stated confirming tripwire did not fire. The one structure worth naming is Amulsar, where OR's stream accrues but pays nothing until a $150 million Armenian government loan and OR's own loan are repaid - a disclosed subordination, and it carries almost no weight in the base case.
apex_basket.skeptic_corrections: One load-bearing correction, plus two footnotes. FOOTNOTE 1: net debt as filed at 30 June 2026 is $143.7 million including finance leases, not the $139.4 million revolver-only figure the record uses - a $0.02 per share difference, and the record's direction and magnitude are right. FOOTNOTE 2: the record attributes the 'remediation complete in the third quarter, mining resumes in the fourth' timetable to Agnico Eagle's 2 July release; that release explicitly declined to give a timetable, and the schedule was published in Agnico Eagle's 29 July second-quarter results. The substance is correct, the date is not. NOTE ON THE CONCLUSION: the correction does not rescue the thesis. The shares are $33.54 today, not $31.19, so upside to the corrected fair value is 11.8% against the record's 12%, and downside to the unchanged $20 adverse case is 40%. The record's 'good business, fair price' verdict survives its own numbers being moved.

apex_basket.value_chain_position: Diversified major - iron ore about 55% of revenue, plus copper, aluminium and lithium - selling raw ore, concentrate and metal; legal two-chain membership within this book.
apex_basket.physical_anchor: Mines and ships iron ore, copper concentrate and cathode, and bauxite and aluminium from operations on five continents.
apex_basket.thesis: Rio Tinto is the cheapest of the large diversified miners once its earnings are measured correctly, holds a first-quartile cost position in both of its main businesses, and for the first time earns more than half its profit from copper, aluminium and lithium rather than iron ore.
apex_basket.cost_curve: The screen's 36.2% margin is a data artifact - Rio reports half-yearly and the automated trailing calculation summed four reporting periods instead of two - so the verified figure is used: roughly 46% ($28.6B of underlying cash operating profit on $61.7B of revenue), with Pilbara iron ore guided at $23.5-25.0 a tonne against a seaborne price near $93, and copper net unit costs cut to 30-50 cents a pound on 15 July 2026 from 65-75 cents. Iron ore, not copper, drives the torque figure: a plus-or-minus 10% commodity move swings cash profit by plus-or-minus 24.9%, and the minus 24.9% is the number to hold in mind, because part of that copper cost cut is a record gold by-product credit that reverses if gold falls.
apex_basket.contracting_reserve: Multi-decade Pilbara reserves plus Simandou's 1.5 billion tonnes at 65-66% iron with about twenty years of life and Gudai-Darri with more than forty; copper life extends through Oyu Tolgoi averaging about 500,000 tonnes a year from 2028 to 2036. Iron ore sells on an index, so no contracted book cushions the downside torque above.
apex_basket.capital_discipline: Net debt of $14.1B against about $28.6B of annual underlying cash profit - roughly half a turn - and this cycle it walked away from a Glencore merger on price, bought Arcadium near the lithium bottom, and refused to be a forced seller of its titanium dioxide and borates units. The counterweight is history: Alcan in 2007 is the sector's canonical top-of-cycle purchase, and Simandou is a large build into a strong tape.
apex_basket.valuation_guard: Base fair value of $104 against a $99.08 price and a reconciled margin-of-safety reading of about plus 2.5% - thin, so the guard passes without granting anything. The adverse case at $62 is 37% below. The cheapness that does exist is genuine rather than accounting: on the corrected earnings base this is about 7.2 times enterprise value to cash profit against BHP at 8.6 and Southern Copper at 16.7.
apex_basket.regime_fit: Both chains it rides read neutral in the cycle sidecar. Its iron-ore half is the leg most exposed to Chinese steel demand, and the reconciled valuation already discounts that structurally by valuing iron ore at 5.0 times against 8.5 times for copper; the copper and aluminium halves are what earn the seat.
apex_basket.phase_fit: A phase of imposed positive real rates rewards payback speed, and this is a business that paid a $3.4B interim dividend out of $3.8B of first-half free cash flow. It is also the seat most open to the criticism the phase note makes: Simandou and lithium are resource optionality, which is the cohort the phase disfavours, so the seat is opened below a full unit and entered on weakness.
apex_basket.decision_rationale: First-half results on 28 July 2026 showed underlying cash operating profit up 28% to $14.8B and free cash flow up 75% to $3.8B, with $870M of productivity benefits banked by 30 June against a $650M promise and the year-end target raised to $1.8B; it takes the eighth seat because its verified trailing margin is about ten points above what the screen printed.
apex_basket.skeptic_kill_fact: No kill fact found. Every load-bearing fact in the bear case verifies against a primary source. (a) COST-CURVE: the cost claim is NOT a proxy artifact - the 2026 Q2 production report (Business Wire 14 July 2026 US / 15 July AEST, filed as a Form 6-K exhibit) carries company guidance of copper net cash unit costs of 30-50 US cents/lb, cut from 65-75 cents, with Rio's own stated reason being higher than expected gold prices plus productivity, and Pilbara cash unit costs of US$23.5-25.0 per wet tonne; the 28 July 2026 half-year call confirms iron ore is 'on track to deliver full year unit costs within guidance'. The record's caveat that a cost guide moving with a by-product metal price is not a cost position stands, and is Rio's own disclosure. (b) RESERVE/CONTRACT: nothing stale or narrative-only found that breaks the case; the opposite - the 28 July call discloses that Kennecott's approved mine life 'officially ends in 2032' with the Apex life-extension to the 2040s still a study ('that decision will be coming in the not-too-distant future'), i.e. the asset carrying the base-case 40-50% copper growth is not yet reserve-backed past 2032, a fact the record does not use. (c) CYCLICAL-PEAK CHEAPNESS: the peak-cycle trap is the record's own conclusion and the chain state corroborates it - this book's own commodity_macro.json (generated 2026-08-11) scores copper_mining setup 0.1/30 with momentum at the 95.8th percentile and diversified_miners setup 1.5/30 with momentum at the 77.4th, i.e. price at the top of its 6y range on maximum momentum. Copper $6.6353/lb and gold $4,436.50/oz on 11 August 2026 confirm the price set is not normalised. (d) HIDDEN DISQUALIFIER: none found. No reserve downgrade, no permit revocation, no disguised streaming/royalty loan; diluted share count went 1,632.4m (Q4 2024) to 1,640.2m (Q2 2026), +0.5% over two years, so there is no serial equity dilution funding the capex step-up. The Mongolian shareholder loan is disclosed and Rio is the lender, not the borrower. The nearest thing to an undisclosed structural risk is new, and it cuts the record's way: incremental unionisation across Pilbara sites for the first time in about 30 years, raised by UBS on the 28 July 2026 call, is a live threat to the first-quartile cost position the whole valuation rests on.
apex_basket.skeptic_corrections:
1) LOAD-BEARING CONFLATION IN THE DATA WARNING (the record's single most emphatic claim). The record asserts the automated bundle is inflated 2x and concludes 'roughly 13.4 times earnings and a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield, not the 7.2 times and 6.8% the bundle implies'. Half of that verifies and half does not. Verified: FMP's independent TTM metrics on 11 August 2026 read free-cash-flow yield 3.47% and earnings yield 7.34% (P/E 13.6), so the 6.8% FCF yield and the $13.67 diluted EPS in the bundle were indeed double-counted (Rio reports half-yearly; four periods were summed). NOT verified: the 7.2x was never a doubling artifact. FMP's TTM EV/EBITDA is 7.40x and TTM EV/sales 2.894x on EV $178.5B, which back-solves to TTM revenue of $61.7B - the same undoubled revenue the record itself calls the true figure. A doubled EBITDA would have printed ~4.3x, not 7.2x. So 13.6x earnings and 7.2-7.4x EV/EBITDA are both true simultaneously; they are different measures, not a corrupted one and a corrected one. The record's rhetorical pairing wrongly tars the peer-comparison anchor (Rio 7.2x vs BHP 8.6x, Vale 8.4x) that its own SoP sanity-check leans on. This corrects the narrative, not the schedule: no valuation level moves, so corrections_typed is empty.
2) DATED INPUTS HAVE MOVED SINCE as_of 2026-08-04, both against two named bear reversion triggers. Gold is $4,436.50/oz on 11 August 2026 versus the $4,152 the record uses, +6.8% in a week, so the gold by-product credit inside the 30-50c copper guide is currently larger, not smaller; the record's 'gold reverting toward $3,000' is a horizon claim, not a near-term one. Brent is $88.76 versus the $79.26 the record cites for 4 August, +12%, so the valley_of_death statement that the diesel headwind 'is now reversing hard into the second half' is no longer true. Both are small in dollars (Rio's own sensitivity is about $0.15/t per $10/bbl, roughly $50m a year on ~330Mt) and neither moves a valuation level.
3) PRICE AND RANGE ANCHORS ARE STALE, IN THE RECORD'S FAVOUR. RIO trades at $100.86 on 11 August 2026 (52-week range now $60.22-$112.58, not the $59.49 low cited). Base-case upside to the unchanged $104 is now +3.1%, not the ~5% stated, and the identified asymmetry widens from about 7:1 to about 12:1 against ($38.86 of downside to the $62 adverse case per $3.14 of base-case upside). The risk_reward verdict of 'poor' is understated, not overstated.
4) BALANCE-SHEET INPUTS RE-DERIVED AND HELD. The filed 30 June 2026 balance sheet (accepted 29 July 2026) shows total debt $22.85B against cash and short-term investments of $9.51B, net debt $13.94B versus the $14.1B company-reported figure the SoP deducts - a $0.10/share difference. Diluted weighted shares are 1,640,167,000, exactly the 1,640m divisor used. Book minority interest is $6.24B, matching the record's $6B deduction (an EV-basis mark on the ~$1.1B/yr of earnings attributable to minorities would be higher, but the record's Oyu Tolgoi shareholder-loan argument is factually correct and offsets it). Re-derived base fair value is $103.7, i.e. $104 unchanged.
5) TWO OMISSIONS THAT STRENGTHEN THE CASE RATHER THAN WEAKEN IT. (i) The record repeatedly frames capex against 'sustaining capital of about $4B' as the mandatory floor; on the 28 July 2026 call Cunningham guided the first-priority bucket (sustaining plus replacement plus decarbonisation) at '$7 billion to $8 billion a year', so the non-discretionary call in a downturn is $3-4B/yr larger than the record assumes. (ii) Kennecott's approved life ends 2032 and the Apex extension is un-FID'd, while the base-case copper leg capitalises 40-50% Kennecott growth at 8.5x.
6) MINOR: the record puts iron ore at 'about 46%' of first-half group earnings; the segment split ($6.8B iron ore of $15.8B product-group EBITDA) and management's own '[n]early 60% of EBITDA... from copper, aluminium and lithium' (28 July 2026) put it nearer 43%. Immaterial to the SoP, which values the segments directly.
7) CATALYST STATUS VERIFIED AS DESCRIBED. SOFT_EXTENDED is correct: the 27 July 2026 Dampier desalination agreements are explicitly non-binding, and on 28 July 2026 Trott said only 'targeting $5 billion of announcements this year' with nothing signed ('No, progressing'). The ~$900m Mongolian tax claim was confirmed by Cunningham as being in a formal arbitration process with no public hearing date, so it remains unschedulable and unsizable as stated.

apex_basket.value_chain_position: Polymetallic base-metal producer - sells copper concentrate as the dominant product with meaningful zinc, gold and silver by-product credits.
apex_basket.physical_anchor: Operates open-pit and underground mines - Constancia in Peru, Snow Lake in Manitoba, Copper World in Arizona - producing copper concentrate with zinc, gold and silver by-products.
apex_basket.thesis: Hudbay mines copper concentrate in Peru, Manitoba and British Columbia at a verified first-quartile cost - a negative cash cost per pound once by-product credits are counted - with reserve lives extended into the 2040s and effectively no net debt.
apex_basket.cost_curve: The screened 66.5% margin is about fifteen points too high: trailing profit embeds a $322M non-cash Copper World impairment reversal from the September 2025 quarter, and the honest adjusted figure is 51%. The cost claim itself is verified - 2026 cash cost guidance improved on 29 July 2026 to minus $0.45 to minus $0.25 per pound of copper, with a June 2026 quarter actual of minus $0.40 against a $1.39 sustaining cash cost. A plus-or-minus 10% copper move swings cash profit by plus-or-minus 11.3%, and that minus 11.3% is absorbable precisely because it is taken from a first-quartile position - that is what separates torque worth owning from a coin flip.
apex_basket.contracting_reserve: Reserve lives run into the 2040s at Constancia and Snow Lake and Copper World is permitted; against that, concentrate sells on annual smelter terms with no long-dated contract cushion, and the depletion of high-grade Pampacancha ore in late 2025 removed the gold by-product credits that flattered earlier quarters - which is why margin fell from 48.6% in the March quarter to 41.0% in June 2026.
apex_basket.capital_discipline: Net debt of 0.04 times cash profit - effectively unlevered - with interest cover of 9.4 times. The risk ahead is the Copper World build, which is exactly the point in a cycle where this sector historically overreaches; the seat is sized on the assumption that it will be funded from cash flow.
apex_basket.valuation_guard: Base fair value of $26.75 against a $24.765 price and a reconciled margin-of-safety reading of about plus 8% - the guard passes, but the deduction is real: strip the impairment reversal and the stock is 8.6 times enterprise value to cash profit rather than the screened 6.6 times, so part of the apparent cheapness was an accounting artifact. The adverse case at $14.50 is 41% below.
apex_basket.regime_fit: Copper reads neutral in the sidecar, and this is the seat built to sit through a neutral chain: a bottom-quartile cost position bounds the downside without needing the metal to rise, and the two-year measured beta of 1.02 confirms it is a genuine copper producer rather than a hedged one.

The growth-and-cooling-inflation quadrant favours demand-linked metals such as copper on volume, which is a reason to be comfortable holding the seat - not a reason to size it larger, since the macro layer moves nothing here.

apex_basket.thesis: Cameco owns the best assets in the nuclear fuel chain - the world's highest-grade uranium orebodies, scarce conversion licences and roughly 230 million pounds committed under long-term contracts - and it is the only seat in this book that does not ride the global-growth and China-demand axis.

A plus-or-minus 10% uranium move swings cash profit by plus-or-minus 30.2%, and that minus 30.2% is the second-largest downside torque in the book - the contracted volumes are what stop it being a coin flip. The beta is an exchange-traded-fund regression, so read it softly.
apex_basket.contracting_reserve: Roughly 230 million pounds committed under long-term contracts - the strongest contracted position in this slate and the canonical tell of where the uranium cycle stands - against McArthur River and Cigar Lake reserves that run for decades. The conversion licences are effectively unreplicable, which is a second and separate scarcity.
apex_basket.capital_discipline: Net cash, at minus 0.1 times cash profit, with interest cover of 9.6 times. It restarted idled capacity rather than building new mines into a rising price, which is the discipline this sector usually lacks and the reason a failing valuation guard does not end the seat.
apex_basket.valuation_guard: The guard is the binding constraint. The reconciled margin-of-safety reading is about minus 21% and the base value of roughly $62 sits well below the $94.06 price, with the adverse case at $40, some 57% below. apex_basket.regime_fit: The uranium chain reads neutral in the sidecar, and the contracted book is what a neutral chain calls for: a producer selling spot into a soft term market owns the downside torque with no cushion, and this one does not.
apex_basket.phase_fit: The growth-and-cooling-inflation quadrant favours demand-linked metals on volume, and reactor fuel is bought on utility schedules rather than on the economic cycle - which is why this seat is the diversifier of the book rather than a second bet on the same thing. Under a phase that rewards payback speed, its raised unit cost of sales is the honest mark against it.

apex_basket.skeptic_corrections: THREE corrections, none fatal, two of which cut against the record's own bear framing. (1) COST METRIC MISLABELLED (load-bearing on this lane's cost-curve test). 'Unit cost of sales rose 36% to C$62.21 per pound' conflates two separate disclosed lines. Reported uranium average unit cost of sales (including depreciation and amortisation) was C$70.81/lb in Q2 2026, up 26% from C$56.19/lb; the produced-and-purchased cash cost was C$62.21/lb, up 36% from C$45.66/lb. The correct cost level is C$8.60/lb HIGHER than stated and the correct growth rate is 10pp LOWER. Direction of the cost-curve drift (up the curve, on a raised full-year guide) is confirmed; the magnitude claim as written is not. No valuation level moves because both sum-of-the-parts cases already assume ~C$70-75 costs. (2) THE GOVERNMENT HAIRCUT IS APPLIED AS A CERTAINTY WHEN IT IS UNVESTED. The record deducts 20% of the US$6.5B above US$17.5B from the base Westinghouse leg as though the US government's participation interest were live. It is not. The 2025-10-28 announcement grants the interest 'once vested', and Grant Isaac on the 2026-07-31 call stated the Department of Commerce partnership 'had two important vesting conditions in it. And the first vesting condition was that it was the responsibility of the Department of Commerce to arrange financing of a minimum $80 billion to support the development of AP1000... That would be the trigger that we would look for under that participation interest.' The record itself concedes the definitive agreements remain unsigned. Applying an unvested contingent claim at 100% understates base fair value. Probability-weighting it at 50% raises the Westinghouse leg from US$25.53 to US$26.27 per share and the base sum from US$59.2 to US$59.9, which on the record's own rounding convention lifts base fair value from US$62 to US$63. The favorable case is unchanged: at a US$45B listing the US$80B financing condition is effectively satisfied by construction, so the full deduction stands. The adverse case is unchanged: at a US$16B listing the value sits below the US$17.5B threshold and no deduction arises either way. (3) THE 'NO CONTRACTED BACKLOG' LIMB IS STALE AS OF THE Q2 2026 FILING. The record argues Westinghouse rests on '91 identified reactor opportunities and at least US$80B of planned investment, neither of which is contracted backlog.' Cameco's Q2 2026 MD&A does disclose Westinghouse contracted backlog and new orders entered: Bernstein's Bob Brackett interrogated those disclosed figures on the 2026-07-31 call, management defined backlog as 'at a point in time of December 31, how much contracted business does Westinghouse have for delivery and revenue recognition in the future', and separately disclosed AP1000 two-pack unit economics of US$14-17B. A filed backlog number therefore exists and the claim that the registration statement will reveal contracted backlog 'for the first time' is wrong. This weakens one supporting limb; it does not touch the multiple argument, which is the load-bearing one. NOT A CORRECTION BUT A STALENESS FLAG FOR THE DIRECTOR: the record's live price of US$94.06 (as-of 2026-08-04) is stale. CCJ traded US$98.18 on 2026-08-11 (market cap US$42.8B), +4.4% since the as-of, on no company-specific news. The gap to the corrected base fair value of US$63 widens from 34% to 36%, so the price objection is stronger now, not weaker.

A plus-or-minus 10% copper move swings cash profit by plus-or-minus 13.5%, and the minus 13.5% understates the true exposure, because a fall in copper would most likely arrive alongside a fall in the by-product metals now doing the work.

apex_basket.phase_fit: The phase note favours copper on both of its axes, and this seat is deliberately not sized on that: the macro read moves nothing here. apex_basket.skeptic_kill_fact: No kill fact found. I attacked the four load-bearing pillars of the bear/pass case against primary sources and each survived. COST-CURVE TRUTH: the company's own 2026-07-22 Q2 call states the operating cash cost per pound BEFORE by-product credits was $2.29 and the cost AFTER credits was $0.05, with a total by-product credit of $1,106 million or $2.24 per pound - the record's central claim that the near-zero headline cost is a by-product artifact, not a mining-cost improvement, is management's own arithmetic, not an inference. CYCLICAL-PEAK CHEAPNESS: the valuation guard is failing for the right reason. On live 2026-08-11 data SCCO trades at 16.39x TTM EV/EBITDA against Freeport at 11.62x and Teck at 7.45x, and the denominator is itself a peak - the Q2 LME copper average was $6.04/lb versus $4.32 a year earlier, silver $73.49/oz (+118%), molybdenum $29.44/lb (+43%), zinc $1.57/lb (+31%), while EVERY product fell in volume (copper -3.5%, moly -11%, silver -4%, zinc -14%) and total operating costs rose $202 million. A 41% revenue increase on four simultaneous multi-year-high prices and falling tons is a price event, and the record refuses to capitalise it. VOLUME: management confirmed on the call that 2026 is 917,000 tons and that 2027 copper will be 'more or less the same', so the third-consecutive-flat-to-down-year claim is verbatim guidance. BALANCE SHEET / FCF: the record's $1.2bn net debt is correct on the filed 30-June-2026 balance sheet ($7,994.4m long-term debt + $534.4m capitalised leases - $7,329.9m cash and short-term investments = $1,198.9m); FMP's own netDebt field of $2,863.8m simply omits the $1,664.9m of short-term investments. And the record's data correction is independently confirmed: the Q2-2026 capital-expenditure sign IS flipped in the source feed (capitalExpenditure +$441.9m, freeCashFlow $2,430.4m), which inflates the TTM figure to $5,965.1m; computed correctly, TTM operating cash flow $6,736.9m less capex $1,655.6m = $5.08bn, an $883.8m overstatement - the record caught this before I did. HIDDEN DISQUALIFIER search found none that breaks the case: no reserve downgrade, no equity issuance (the $1.25bn 10-year 5.35% June note covers most of Tia Maria's $1.8bn), no royalty or streaming structure, and the permit/licence issues that exist (illegal miners obstructing Los Chancas; the El Pilar water licence, now renewed) are already netted to zero in the record's own parts valuation.
apex_basket.skeptic_corrections: Four corrections, none of which moves the fair-value level. (1) STALE SILVER - load-bearing to the timing argument, not to the valuation. The record asserts silver 'trades at $60.14 an ounce today', 18% below the $73.49 Q2 average that produced the credit. Silver closed at $60.245 on 2026-08-04 (the record's as-of date) but has rallied to $64.92 on 2026-08-11, so the gap is 11.7%, not 18%. The record's own sizing of the hit (~$270m annualised on 9% of sales at near-100% incremental margin) should read ~$175m. The direction of the argument survives; the magnitude is a third smaller than stated. (2) THE PRE-CREDIT UNIT COST HAS ALREADY INFLECTED DOWN. The record repeatedly frames pre-credit cash cost as 'rising 12% in five quarters, from $2.05 to $2.29'. True over five quarters, but the company said on 2026-07-22 that the $2.29 was '$0.02 lower than the value for the first quarter of this year' ($2.31), a 1% sequential DECLINE driven by lower production and administrative cost per pound and higher premiums. The base case's $2.35/lb and the adverse case's $2.40/lb therefore both sit above the latest actual print - the record has penalised itself by ~$0.06/lb, worth roughly +$1.8/share, which is why I am not moving the level. (3) THE CREDIT COMPRESSION IS NOT A FUTURE EVENT - IT ALREADY HAPPENED ONCE WITHOUT DAMAGE. The record's forcing function says the credit reversal first meets the numbers in the late-October Q3 report. In fact the by-product credit already fell 7% sequentially, from $1,189m ($2.41/lb) in Q1 2026 to $1,106m ($2.24/lb) in Q2, and EBITDA still set a record and the shares still made highs. The Q3 print is therefore a weaker forcing function than the record claims; a single quarter of credit compression has already been absorbed. (4) AN UNSOURCED DATE. The catalyst note and forcing function state Tia Maria 'commissioning tests targeted for May or June 2027 ... (second-quarter 2026 call)'. That detail does not appear in the 2026-07-22 transcript, which says only 'hopefully in the later part of 2027'; on that same call a Goldman Sachs analyst noted the disclosure had moved from 'third quarter of 2027' on the prior call to 'second half' in this release, and management answered 'for now, we don't expect a delay'. Attribute the May/June date to an earlier call or drop it - the softening from Q3-2027 to 2H-2027 is the better-supported point and cuts the record's way. Two footnotes: company-reported adjusted EBITDA was $2,856m at a 67% margin versus the record's computed $2,849m/66.4%; and the 0.012 stock dividend declared 2026-07-16 has a record date of 2026-08-11 (today), which has already restated the 52-week range in the data feed (high $221.67 -> $219.04, low $90.11 -> $89.04) - the record's levels, struck against a pre-adjustment $195.475, correspond to about $98.8/$154.1/$215.4 post-adjustment, a uniform 1.2% that leaves every ratio in the record intact.

mining_memo:
MINING BOOK, LANE A - DIRECTOR'S MEMO, 11 AUGUST 2026

(a) How the names were scored, and what valuation was allowed to do

Four pillars of twenty-five points each, applied only to names that cleared the gates. First,
cost-curve position and the quality of the torque - how much cash profit moves for a 10% move in
the commodity, and whether that swing is taken from a low-cost or a marginal position. Second, the
contracting cycle and reserve life, which for a royalty company means the paying-asset book. Third,
capital discipline and the balance sheet - this sector's besetting sin is building at the top, so
last-cycle behaviour is scored, not just today's leverage. Fourth, a valuation guard.

The guard is a guard, not a ranking pillar. Every name starts with full marks and loses them only
for danger: a price well above the reconciled value of the parts, or earnings struck on a peak
commodity price that must be normalised before any cheapness is credited. It vetoed one name, capped
several, and in no case lifted a name above another that passed clean. Teck is the clearest
illustration - it carries the largest discount in the universe, about 29%, and it is a runner-up, not
a seat, because a discount cannot buy rank.

Catalysts played no part. This book has the event overlay fully removed: a live catalyst is neither
a plus nor a requirement, and the dated-event book is elsewhere.

One methodological point that changed several rankings materially. Where the debate verified
company-reported cost and margin figures against the automated screen and the two disagreed, the
company figure won, as the rubric requires. That correction cut Hudbay (the screened 66.5% margin
embeds a $322M non-cash impairment reversal; the honest figure is 51%), cut Southern Copper's
cost-curve credit (the near-zero cash cost is a by-product credit, not a mining achievement), and
lifted Rio Tinto by roughly ten points of margin (the screen summed four half-year periods instead of
two) and Vale (the screened 25% margin and 1.5 times net debt are both corrupted by December 2025
non-cash charges; the true figures are about 42% and 0.97 times).

(b) Excluded and capped

By the credibility gate:
  - Alamos Gold - excluded outright, credibility scored two out of five with a turning trajectory.
    Its own 29 July 2026 revision lifted 2026 all-in sustaining cost guidance 18% at the midpoint to
    $1,775-1,875 an ounce while the screen still filed it in the high-margin cohort. Not eligible at
    any price. No other name in the universe was gated, and none was capped for a worsening
    trajectory.

By the solvency gate:
  - No eligible name reads weak on funded debt, so the gate excluded nobody. Alcoa and Teck read
    moderate, which passes; Teck's own 30 June 2026 balance sheet in fact shows net cash of C$1,244
    million, which the screen missed entirely.

By the valuation guard:
  - Franco-Nevada - vetoed. A reconciled margin-of-safety reading of about minus 53%, past the level
    at which the reconciled fair value cannot reach the price. A superb business - a cash cost of $341
    per gold-equivalent ounce, roughly a fifth of a typical producer's all-in cost - at a price this
    book will not pay.
  - Wheaton Precious Metals - capped out at about minus 26%, and blocked independently by the
    three-name limit on the precious-metals chain.
  - Southern Copper - seated but cut to 0.40 units, the smallest seat, on a guard reading of about
    minus 10% and a price roughly 20% above the reconciled value of the parts.
  - Cameco - seated at 0.50 units on a guard reading of about minus 21%; kept for its contract book
    and because it is the only separate risk in the basket, with fresh money held back for evidence.
  - Agnico Eagle - trimmed to 0.50 units on a guard reading of about minus 10%, with earnings struck
    at a gold price that has already begun to fall.
  - Freeport-McMoRan, Ero Copper, Buenaventura and Fortuna Mining - all deducted for a price above
    the reconciled value or for a cost position their own disclosures show to be mid-curve; none
    seated.
  - Alcoa - not seated. Worst cost position in its cohort, an alumina business losing $96M a quarter,
    interest cover of 3.5 times. A taxonomy note for the map while we are here: it is a metal
    converter filed in the copper chain and benchmarked against orebody miners whose margins are
    structurally far higher, so its bottom-of-cohort band overstates the case against it - it is not
    seated on the merits either way.

By the headwind rule:
  - Nobody. Every chain reads neutral in the cycle sidecar, so no seat is clamped by the headwind
    rule and no headwind justification is required or given. The macro note's separate view that
    monetary metals are currently out of favour is a macro read; by this book's rules it cannot move
    a size, and it has not.

Split rule and physical anchors: every name in the input is a producer or a royalty company. No
equipment, services or utility name reached this desk, so there is nothing to report as a
map-merge failure, and every seat carries a specific physical anchor - ore mined, metal poured, or a
contractual claim on ounces produced by a named third party.

(c) Downside torque, seat by seat

Torque cuts both ways, and every seat whose case cites it carries the downside number here.

  - OR Royalties: plus-or-minus 9.7% cash profit per 10% gold move. Downside minus 9.7%, taken from
    a 96.8% cash margin - the lowest-cost position in the book, so the swing is survivable.
  - Rio Tinto: plus-or-minus 24.9%. Downside minus 24.9%, driven by iron ore rather than copper, and
    part of the recent copper cost cut is a gold by-product credit that reverses with the metal.
  - Royal Gold: plus-or-minus 12.7%. Downside minus 12.7% with no cost to cut - a royalty book has
    no operating lever.
  - Hudbay: plus-or-minus 11.3%. Downside minus 11.3%, absorbed from a verified negative cash cost
    per pound - the reason this torque is compounding leverage rather than a coin flip.
  - Agnico Eagle: plus-or-minus 13.2%. Downside minus 13.2%, and it is already happening: the
    realised price fell from about $4,900 to $4,483 between the March and June 2026 quarters.
  - Vale: plus-or-minus 31.9%. Downside minus 31.9% - the largest in the book - with no contracted
    book beneath it, and the beta behind it is an index regression, so read it softly.
  - Cameco: plus-or-minus 30.2%. Downside minus 30.2%, bounded only by roughly 230 million pounds of
    committed long-term contracts; the beta is an exchange-traded-fund regression, so read it softly.
  - Southern Copper: plus-or-minus 13.5%. Downside minus 13.5%, and it understates the true risk,
    because a copper fall would most likely arrive with a fall in the silver and molybdenum credits
    now producing the near-zero headline cost.

(d) Shared commodity factors, and how each was resolved

The shared global-growth and China-demand axis, decomposed first as required. Four of the eight seats
ride it: Hudbay and Southern Copper through copper, Rio Tinto and Vale through seaborne iron ore into
Chinese steel. The measured two-year weekly correlations say these are not four independent bets -
Hudbay against Southern Copper is 0.82, Vale against Southern Copper 0.74, Hudbay against Vale 0.61,
against a book-wide average pairwise figure of 0.57. A China demand shock or a global-growth
downgrade hits all four in the same week. Resolved by keeping with an explicit cap rather than by
diversifying, for the arithmetic reason set out below, and the cap is numeric: the four names are
capped at 2.25 units combined and the two copper names at 1.05 units combined. Southern Copper - the
lowest-scoring seat in the book and the name appearing in both measured breaches - is cut from 0.6 to
0.4 units, the smallest position here.

The gold and real-rate axis. Three of the eight seats ride it: Royal Gold, OR Royalties and Agnico
Eagle. These are the most damning numbers on the page - Royal Gold against Agnico Eagle 0.86, OR
against Agnico Eagle 0.86, Royal Gold against OR 0.84. Two of them are one bet, and the royalties are
emphatically not a diversifier of the producer; all three de-rate together on a real-rate move.
Resolved by keeping with a cap of 2.00 units combined, achieved by cutting Agnico Eagle - the
lowest-scoring of the three, the only one whose price sits above the reconciled value of its parts,
and the only one with no moat in its file - from 0.7 to 0.5 units.

Why diversification was not available on either axis. After the credibility exclusion, seventeen
names remain and they occupy only four chains: precious metals, copper, diversified miners and the
uranium fuel cycle. There is not one rare-earth or strategic-metals name in the input, and exactly one
uranium name, which is already seated. With a limit of three names per chain, and with the only
diversified-miners name that is not also a copper name being Vale, the arithmetic closes: the maximum
number of distinct seats reachable without a fourth copper name is seven, unless the precious-metals
chain carries three. An eight-name slate therefore forces a three-plus-three-plus-two-plus-one shape,
and no swap inside that shape removes an axis - it only exchanges one name on the axis for another.
That is why both resolutions are caps rather than swaps, and it is stated rather than glossed.

The uranium contracting cycle. One seat, Cameco, so no action is required; it is named because the
instruction requires every chain-specific axis to be reported. It is the one genuinely separate risk
in this basket, and the reason its size went up rather than down.

Export controls and rare earths. Zero seats, because the eligible universe contains no rare-earth or
strategic-metals name at all. Reported for completeness; no action is possible.

One standing note on gold. This system does not score the gold price anywhere, by design - the
momentum guard exists because a price-following rule would have bought the January 2026 top. Nothing
above ranks a seat because gold rose.

(e) Rise and fall against the prior slate

The prior apex, dated 4 August 2026, carried seven seats: Royal Gold 80, Hudbay 78, OR Royalties 77,
Agnico Eagle 76, Vale 70, Southern Copper 66, Cameco 60, with Teck 74, Rio Tinto 68, Fortuna 66,
Wheaton 65, Buenaventura 63 and Ero 60 in reserve. This run:

  - OR Royalties 77 to 83. Up six: the 8 July 2026 disclosure confirmed a 96.8% cash margin and 2030
    volumes contracted, and the correction to the impossible screened margin left the conclusion
    intact.
  - Rio Tinto 68 to 82, promoted from reserve. Up fourteen, almost all of it a data correction - the
    screen had summed four half-year periods instead of two, understating the trailing margin by
    about ten points - plus verified first-quartile costs on both legs and a 28 July 2026 result
    showing cash profit up 28% and free cash flow up 75%.
  - Royal Gold 80 to 81. Up one: the 21 July 2026 disclosure of $871 per gold-equivalent ounce
    against $4,506 realised confirmed the widest cash spread in the book.
  - Hudbay 78 to 76. Down two: the cost claim was verified and improved, but the screened margin
    proved about fifteen points too high once the September 2025 impairment reversal is stripped, and
    the stock is 8.6 rather than 6.6 times cash profit.
  - Agnico Eagle 76 to 73. Down three: the cost position is still the best in the senior tier, but the
    advantage over Newmont is about $220 an ounce rather than the hundreds management claims, margin
    rolled over 4.2 points in the June quarter, and the price sits above the reconciled value.
  - Vale 70 to 73. Up three on net: the corrected margin (42%, not 25%) and net debt (0.97 times, not
    1.5) are materially better than the screen showed, partly offset by the 31 July 2026 increase in
    both cash and all-in cost guidance.
  - Cameco 60 to 67. Up seven: the contract book at roughly 230 million pounds is the strongest
    contracted position in the slate and the adjusted margin is 54% rather than the screened 24.9%;
    held back by unit cost of sales up 36% year over year.
  - Southern Copper 66 to 65. Down one, and the composition changed more than the number: the reserve
    life and return on capital still score well, but the near-zero cash cost turned out to be a $2.24
    by-product credit while the underlying mining cost rose from $2.05 to $2.29 a pound.

Reserve list changes: Teck 74 to 77 and Rio Tinto promoted out of it; BHP added at 72 (the 16 July
2026 operational review confirmed a sixth consecutive year as lowest-cost iron-ore major); Wheaton 65
to 70; Ero 60 to 63; Freeport enters at 58. Fortuna and Buenaventura drop off the reserve list -
both were shown by their own disclosures to be mid- or high-cost operators enjoying a high metal
price, Fortuna at $2,157 per gold-equivalent ounce against guidance of $1,830-1,975.

(f) Rotation, reconciled to the ledger

The ledger records seven held names and no drops this year. This run drops nothing, re-adds nothing,
adds one, and re-sizes six.

  - OR Royalties - KEEP at 0.75 units. Thesis untouched; 96.8% cash margin confirmed 8 July 2026.
  - Royal Gold - KEEP at 0.75 units, which is also the ceiling the mid-build cash-flow flag imposes.
    $871 per gold-equivalent ounce disclosed 21 July 2026.
  - Hudbay - KEEP, trimmed 0.8 to 0.65. Cost guidance improved 29 July 2026 to a negative cost per
    pound; the trim is for the fifteen-point margin overstatement, not for the thesis.
  - Agnico Eagle - KEEP, trimmed 0.7 to 0.5. Still the lowest-cost senior, but it is the cut leg of
    the gold cap and its realised price has turned.
  - Vale - KEEP, trimmed 0.6 to 0.55. Cost guidance raised 31 July 2026; thesis intact, trend adverse.
  - Southern Copper - KEEP, cut 0.6 to 0.4. Not broken - the price is nowhere near the level that
    would break it, the credibility and solvency files are clean, and the reserve life stands - but it
    is the weakest seat on the rubric and the one in both measured correlation breaches. Teck was
    considered as the strictly-better replacement for this seat and rejected: it scores higher, but it
    sits on the same global-growth and China-demand axis, so the swap would buy quality without
    buying orthogonality, and the discount that makes it attractive is anchored to a pending merger,
    which is not a reason this book owns anything. Teck stays first in reserve.
  - Cameco - KEEP, raised 0.4 to 0.5. Raised because it is the only seat not on a shared axis, not
    because anything in its own numbers improved - its unit cost of sales is going the wrong way.
  - Rio Tinto - ADD at 0.65 units. The eighth seat, required because the slate must carry exactly
    eight. Added on the verified margin correction and the 28 July 2026 half-year result, not on the
    capital-release programme, which remains unsigned and carries no weight in this book.

(g) Bear rebuttal - the strongest reason each seat is wrong, written before final sizing

  - OR Royalties: cleaning the impossible screened margin lifts the multiple from about 16 to about
    20 times cash earnings, so the cheapest-looking royalty in the book is not actually cheap.
  - Rio Tinto: it is a 55%-iron-ore company being seated in the copper chain, and its own valuation
    discounts Chinese steel structurally - if that discount is too small, the largest part of the
    business is worth less than the base case says.
  - Royal Gold: it is the only royalty here carrying debt, it bought the Sandstorm book at a high gold
    price, and the two valuation readings on file disagree with each other.
  - Hudbay: the high-grade Pampacancha ore that supplied the gold credits behind the negative cash
    cost is depleted, so the first-quartile position may already be historical.
  - Agnico Eagle: the shares trade above the reconciled value of the parts on earnings struck at a
    gold price that has fallen 8% in a quarter, and the file records no moat.
  - Vale: cost guidance has now been raised twice in a year while margin compresses on rising revenue,
    and it carries the book's largest downside torque with no contracted cushion.
  - Cameco: unit cost of sales rose 36% year over year, guidance was raised, and the reconciled value
    sits about a third below the market price - the contract book is bounding a thesis that the
    numbers are currently working against.
  - Southern Copper: strip the silver and molybdenum credit and the mining cost rose 12%; the market
    is paying 20% above the reconciled value for a cost position that is borrowed from other metals.

(h) Macro - what it changed, and what it did not

The cited block reads a debt-cycle phase in which the bond market is imposing positive real rates, a
growth-rising and inflation-cooling quadrant, and a neutral risk regime, with a winner scoreboard
placing strategic metals first and the uranium fuel cycle last. It also carries an explicit warning
that the macro layer is degraded - the phase is a seeded prior, not yet earned by the state machine.
That warning is honoured here: unnamed families are treated as neutral, no headwind is read into the
gap, and because a data gap must never tighten the book, nothing was cut on the strength of it.

What it changed. Three things, all of them the sanctioned channels. First, posture: the stance for
this run is cautious, which reflects the phase read alongside the fact that six of the eight seats
trade at or above the reconciled value of their parts. Second, the entry bar: in this quadrant a
fresh entry wants a discount of at least 20% to reconciled value, and no seat in this book clears
that - which is why five of the eight are marked to wait for weakness, two to scale in, and Cameco
to wait for a specific piece of evidence rather than a price. Third, the horizon: eighteen months
rather than twelve, because a phase in which real rates are being imposed lengthens the time a
cost-curve advantage needs to show up in cash rather than in the multiple. Fourth, the per-seat
phase commentary, which is judgement and nothing more - Rio Tinto's Simandou and lithium builds and
Cameco's raised unit costs are both named there as sitting against the phase, and both seats were
taken anyway.

What it did not change. Membership: no name is in or out of this book because of the phase, the
quadrant, or its rank on the scoreboard - the seats were chosen on the four pillars and the gates,
and the shape was forced by the chain caps and the eligible universe. Conviction: no score moved on a
macro citation, and no decision rationale above cites one. Sizing: not one unit was set or moved by
the macro read - the only things that moved sizes were name-specific dated facts (Hudbay's margin
correction, Agnico's falling realised price, Vale's raised cost guidance, Southern Copper's
by-product credit) and the two correlation caps. The clearest test of this is precious metals: the
macro block calls it a headwind family and ranks it second on the scoreboard, and neither fact
touched a single unit - the gold cluster was cut on measured correlation and on Agnico's own price
against its own value, not on the phase. Copper is the mirror image: the block calls it a tailwind
and the top-confidence family, and Southern Copper was still cut to the smallest seat in the book.

Sizing note for the audit trail. This book publishes equal-weighted, so the eight seats each carry
12.5% of published weight regardless of the units above. The chain exposure reported alongside this
memo is therefore the published one: precious metals and copper each carry three of eight seats and
so 37.5%, diversified miners two seats and 25%, the uranium fuel cycle one seat and 12.5%. Both
three-seat chains sit above the 30% weight bound by arithmetic rather than by drift - under equal
weighting three of eight seats is always 37.5% - and both are inside the three-name limit that
actually binds. Measured on the size units instead, precious metals is 42.1%, copper 35.8%,
diversified miners 25.3% and the uranium fuel cycle 10.5%. Those two breaches are stated rather than
engineered away: bringing them under 30% would require sizing Vale and Cameco at roughly double every
other seat, which would misrepresent conviction in the very record that is meant to decide whether
equal weighting is ever switched off.
